title: Graph attention networks
blurb: Learned neighbour weights, softmax, multi-head attention

hook.title: Not every friend deserves equal airtime
hook.text: In a meeting you don't weigh every colleague's opinion equally: the expert on this topic gets more attention than a bystander, and *which* person is the expert depends on the topic. GCN and GraphSAGE give every neighbour the same weight $1/|N(v)|$. A **graph attention network** lets the model *learn* those weights from the messages themselves: score each neighbour, turn scores into a probability distribution, then listen accordingly.
hook.recall: Remember the meeting: attention weights $\alpha_{vu}$ are learned from content, normalised by a softmax over the neighbours, and computed by a shared mechanism, so they work on any graph.

explore.intro: Node $v$ with four neighbours. You control the attention vector $a$; the page shows the softmax weights and the aggregated output.
tasks: Move the sliders so that neighbour $u_4$ dominates. Compare with the uniform GCN weights.
Switch to 3 heads: what is concatenated?
explore.takeaway: $e_{vu}=a(W h_u,Wh_v)$, $\alpha_{vu}=\frac{\exp(e_{vu})}{\sum_{k\in N(v)}\exp(e_{vk})}$, $h_v^{(l)}=\sigma(\sum_{u\in N(v)}\alpha_{vu}W^{(l)}h_u^{(l-1)})$. Multi-head attention stabilises learning.

build.prompt: Order the steps of one graph attention layer for node $v$.
items: Compute attention coefficients $e_{vu}$ for each neighbour from the messages
Normalise them with a softmax into $\alpha_{vu}$ ($\sum_u\alpha_{vu}=1$)
build.explanation: Slides 38–39: compute $e_{vu}$, normalise with softmax, then aggregate with the final attention weights.

questions.prompt: In GCN/GraphSAGE the weight of neighbour $u$ in the aggregation is:
Attention scores for three neighbours are $(\ln2,\,0,\,0)$. What is $\alpha$ for the first neighbour after softmax?
Why are the coefficients $e_{vu}$ passed through a softmax?
options: To reduce the number of neighbours
questions.explanation: A proper probability distribution over the neighbours.

questions.prompt: Which statement about graph attention is FALSE?
options: The approach is agnostic to the choice of $a$ (e.g. a single-layer network)
The parameters of $a$ are trained jointly with $W^{(l)}$
Attention coefficients can be computed in parallel across all edges
Attention must be computed one edge at a time
questions.explanation: Computation of attentional coefficients can be parallelised across all edges.

questions.prompt: What is multi-head attention used for?
options: It can stabilise the learning process of the attention mechanism; heads are aggregated by concatenation or summation
questions.explanation: Several attention replicas with different parameters.

questions.prompt: *“GAT must learn a separate free weight for every edge in the graph, so it cannot be applied to a new graph.”* What’s wrong?
options: $\alpha_{vu}$ comes from a shared edge-wise mechanism $a$ with a fixed number of parameters irrespective of graph size, hence inductive
New graphs always have fewer edges
questions.explanation: Benefits slide: shared edge-wise mechanism; fixed number of parameters; inductive capability.
